name_ru: Тун Му Чжэн Шань Сяо Чжун
processing: Fully oxidised black tea; the traditional version is dried over burning pine, which leaves a smoky aroma. Unsmoked versions are also made.
harvest_season: Spring is usual for the better lots, as with most Wuyi black teas.
appearance_dry: Tight, even strips, iron-dark with a brownish, slightly oily sheen.
taste_profile: Mellow and clearly sweet, with a longan-like richness; smoked versions carry pine smoke woven into that sweetness rather than sitting on top of it.

brewing.notes: Short steeps in a gaiwan keep it sweet. It also takes milk well in a Western pot.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, usually the current or previous spring, in smoked and unsmoked versions that should be labelled as such. Not everything sold under the name is from there, so the village and maker matter more than the label. It keeps a few years if dry and sealed.
description:
This is Lapsang Souchong from its home ground: the Tongmu area in the Wuyi Mountains nature reserve in northern Fujian. The name separates it from 'outside mountain' teas (waishan xiaozhong), which are copies made elsewhere, often from gongfu black tea smoked afterwards.

The area is high and cool, at about 1,200 to 1,500 metres. The leaf was traditionally dried over burning pine and took up the smoke; today both smoked and unsmoked versions are made. One account holds that only seed-grown Wuyi caicha from within Wuyishan qualifies for the name.

A good cup is deep amber and sweet first, with a longan-like richness and, in smoked lots, a pine note that stays calm. Harsh tar or ash points to heavy smoking of weak leaf. Keep steeps short; it also holds up to milk.

When buying, ask whether it is smoked, which year and which village. Plenty of tea carries the name without meeting that standard, so a very low price is a warning.
history:
Accounts usually place the start of small-leaf black tea here in the late Ming, though the often-quoted '400 years' comes mainly from trade and promotional writing rather than close historical study. The tea is also known as Xingcun Xiaozhong, after Xingcun township.

Jin Jun Mei was developed from its methods in 2005.
